1:
Why the rejoicing is forbidden is answered from the occasion. Gill canvasses what they might have been rejoicing over: military success that enlarged their border, a league with a foreign king, or a good harvest; on any of these they should not rejoice as other people do, with illumination of houses, fires in the streets and feasting, since the prosperity would be short-lived; he inclines rather to think it was over their idols. Wesley names the same forms, feastings and triumphs and sacrifices of thanksgiving. Calvin turns the prohibition into a warning about prosperity itself. Hypocrites, so long as God spares them, take occasion to be secure, thinking they have sure peace with him because he bears with them a short time, and until the drawn sword appears they are never afraid; so the prophet tells this people that however bountifully God nourished them the joy would be vain.

What the reward is divides the readers. Ellicott takes the harlot's hire on every corn-floor as bold imagery for the prophet's scorn: the yield of the harvest is called the hire, which lures the faithless bride to worship the false deity from whose hands the gifts were supposed to come. Wesley reads it the same way, so that they loved to see the floor full and said their idols gave the plenty. Henry allows both directions. They may have loved to give rewards to their idols, in the offerings and first-fruits presented out of every corn-floor, taking a strange pleasure in serving them with what they would have grudged to consecrate to God, whence he draws a rule, that those who are niggardly in the expenses of their religion are commonly prodigal in spending upon their lusts; or they may have loved to receive rewards from their idols, reckoning the fruits of the earth to be such. Henry also states why the charge is worded so: their covenant with God was a marriage-covenant, so other nations were idolaters without going a whoring from God as this people did; and the sins of those who have professed religion are more provoking than the sins of others.

Clarke sets out the chapter before glossing it: the prophet reproves them for the rejoicings on their corn-floors, by which they ascribed to idols, as the heathen did, the praise of all their plenty; for this they are threatened with famine and exile in a land where they would be polluted and want the means of worshipping the God of their fathers.

The failure of the harvest is described in several degrees. Gill offers three: that there will not be corn enough on the floor nor wine in the press, whether through blight or an enemy treading them down; or that enough may be got in and then turned into a curse or carried off; or that they may enjoy it and receive no nourishment, looking like starved creatures in the midst of plenty. Ellicott corrects two words, reading wine-vat for winepress, since it is what the new wine flowed into, and preferring deceive her to fail in her, on the authority of two old versions. Calvin makes the deprivation the method rather than the penalty: it is the only way by which the Lord restores men to a sane mind, or at least renders them inexcusable. He illustrates it with the figure already used: a harlot, while the gain lasts and she outshines all honest matrons in dress, is blinded by her own splendour, but when reduced to want she sighs at last and owns how infatuated she was to leave her husband. Keil and Delitzsch marks where the threat is going: having fallen away they will be driven out of the land, the driving away being described as a return to one country while another is named immediately after as the actual place of banishment.
3:
The land itself carries the weight of the threat. Gill explains why Canaan is called the Lord's land: though all the earth is his, this was peculiarly so, chosen for himself and for this people, where he had his temple and caused his divine Majesty to dwell in a special manner, so that the Targum calls it the land of the Shechinah; it is sometimes called Immanuel's land, where the Messiah was to be born and dwell. He notes that Kimchi wrongly interprets it of Jerusalem only, and others of Judea, whereas it designs the whole land of promise, given by promise to the fathers and held by the tenure of obedience to the Lord of the land. Calvin makes the expulsion worse than the famine already threatened. To be deprived of the land of Canaan, which the Psalms call the Lord's rest, was a repudiation: while they dwelt there they lived as it were in the habitations of God, but once expelled the Lord testified that he regarded them as aliens, as when a father disinherits his son. Calvin also points out the play on words, the one verb from dwelling and the other from returning. Clarke passes over the verse with a cross-reference.

Why the unclean food is the worst of it is Calvin's own emphasis. Had the prophet said only that they would pine away with want in a far country, the denunciation would have been grievous enough; but he fills them with much greater horror, because the abstaining from unclean meats was the badge of divine adoption. When the people ate indiscriminately and made no choice according to the law, the distinction was removed and they ceased to be the people of God; it was as though the Lord meant to blend that holy people with the profane Gentiles so that there should afterwards be no difference.

Whether the sacrifices cease or are merely refused divides the readers of the next verse. Gill states both: it may threaten the cessation of sacrifice in a strange land where there is neither temple nor altar, so that as they would not offer when they should, now they shall not if they would; or, with Kimchi, it may reprove their present sacrifices, offered not in faith but hypocritically and before their calves, the future tense being sometimes put for the present, which is the way Schmidt goes. Calvin argues for the second from the context: as long as they lived in their own country they were sedulous enough in outward worship and did not neglect drink-offerings, so the prophet must be speaking of the effect only, that their libation did not come to Jehovah and their labour was fruitless. Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch keep the first: Wesley says the wine-offerings appointed with the morning and evening sacrifice shall all be withheld from these captives, and Keil and Delitzsch that temple and ritual will both be wanting in exile, so that they will be unable to observe any of the feasts of the Lord.

The bread of mourners is explained from the law. Clarke recalls that a dead body and everything related to it, the house and the persons who touched it, were all polluted. Ellicott gets a better rendering by abandoning the Hebrew accentuation, calls it funeral food which defiles for seven days those who partake of it, and reads the last clause as saying their bread is only for bodily sustenance and does not come to Jehovah's house as a sacred offering; he adds that these verses show Hosea did not consider the worship of the Northern Kingdom as in itself illegal, and reports that Kuenen proposes an alteration of the text which makes the parallelism more harmonious. Calvin compares the sacrifices to murders, citing Isaiah that killing an ox is the same as slaying a man.
5:
The question about the feast-days is pressed home in different ways. Gill takes it of the captivity: what would they do in the solemn day, the seventh day of the week appointed for rest and worship, and the feasts of the passover, pentecost and tabernacles, when those who held them captive would not allow them time for such solemnities, nor furnish them with proper sacrifices, nor accommodate them with a place to offer at; so they would learn by sad experience the want of the means of serving the Lord which in their own land they had despised. Clarke adds a detail from Calmet, that the Israelites who remained in the land after its subjection to the Assyrians did worship the true God and offer the sacrifices appointed by the law, though in an imperfect and schismatic manner, and that it was a great mortification to be deprived of their religious festivals in a land of strangers. Wesley says they would not then be suffered to observe any of them.

Calvin makes the silence of the festivals the real sentence. He grants that from the time the place of the temple was changed and spurious rites were introduced by Jeroboam the people were wholly rejected; but as circumcision remained, as sacrifices were offered as it were by Moses' command, and as they lived in the holy land, they were satisfied with their condition. The trumpets sounded on the festivals so that the people might come from the whole land into the temple, and this was as the voice of God sounding from heaven; when the feast-days were forgotten and there were no holy assemblies, it was the same as if the Lord by commanding silence had proved that he no longer cared for the people. So the threat is not exile only but that God would wholly forsake them, and that no token of his presence would remain.

The flight to Egypt is read as already made or as still coming. Gill and Wesley take it as begun, many having gone out of their own land to escape the Assyrian army which invaded the country and besieged Samaria, with the famine Kimchi thinks is meant here. Calvin holds that the prophet speaks of the exile as if it had already taken place when it was only near at hand, setting forth by that manner of speaking the certainty of the prediction. Keil and Delitzsch says the same of the following verse, that its perfects are prophetic, and that when the time of visitation arrives Israel will learn that the prophets who predicted only prosperity and good were infatuated fools.

That Egypt would be a grave rather than a refuge is agreed. Calvin observes that the verb for gathering is used in a bad sense, as we say to pack up or to bundle, and that the burying which follows makes this clearer: the prophet declares not a kind retreat but that Egypt would be a sepulchre in which they should remain shut up, so that those who dreamed of a return would be given a perpetual habitation instead. He adds that nettles and thorns do not grow in an inhabited place, so their absence from the land measures the length of the exile. Clarke says they went there only to die, that Memphis, now Cairo, found them graves, and that the villas purchased with their money lay neglected under nettles and brambles. Ellicott makes Memphis the point of the irony: the vast city and necropolis of Ptah, where Apis and Ibis, kings and men, lay by thousands mummied, the religious shrine of Egyptian faith in the under-world, from which Israel had been emancipated at the Exodus. He reads the silver clause as a longing for the silver left behind concealed in their desolate land, and holds that many exiles did take refuge in Egypt after the northern kingdom was overthrown.
7:
The doubling of the announcement is read as a stroke against security. Gill notes that the days are fixed and appointed by the Lord, and that the clause is repeated for the certainty of it. Calvin says the prophet meant to shake off the supine torpor of hypocrites, who covered themselves over with hardness, so that it was necessary to deal roughly with them; under Jeroboam the second, the son of Joash, their affairs were prosperous, and because the Lord did not immediately visit their sins they thought they had escaped. He adds the old proverb, which Homer also has, that the foolish knows when he suffers: those who will not now submit to teaching are taken to another school, where God teaches not by the mouth but by the hand. Henry sets the two words side by side, a day of visitation in which sins are brought to light, and a day of recompence in which a reward is given to every man according to his work.

Who is called a fool is the difficulty of the verse. Clarke, Wesley and Henry take it of the pretender: Clarke of one who foretold peace and plenty on divine authority and is now enraged to see everything falling out contrary to his prediction; Henry of those who flattered the people in their sins and rocked them asleep in their security. Henry asks why God would suffer his people to be imposed upon by such men, and answers from the verse itself, that because they would not receive the love of the truth but conceived a hatred of it, he sent them strong delusions, which nothing but the day of recompence would undeceive; the same day would show them that the true prophets they had counted madmen were the wise men of their time. Ellicott turns the sentence the other way and renders it crazed is the prophet, mad the inspired one, while persecution is increased, taking this either as the depraved public opinion Hosea scornfully describes or, more probably, as the true prophet driven distracted by the persecutions he suffers. He grants that Maurer and Hitzig, preceded by Jerome and many expositors, read the word as false prophet, but doubts with Nowack whether the Hebrew for inspired one can bear that sense with the definite article; and he ends by saying no decisive superiority can be claimed for any rendering yet proposed.

The watchman divides the readers in the same way. Gill and Wesley supply a past tense, so that formerly the watchmen of Ephraim were with the true God, as Elijah and Elisha were, whereas now they neither are with him nor for him. Calvin says interpreters obscure the verse, almost all of them supposing a verb to be understood, that Ephraim had set a watchman; he sees no need to change the words. He describes the contrast he would have approved, between the old prophets who drew all they taught from the true fountain and the present ones who lay snares and rule in the temple, so that of the sacred temple of God they make a brothel for the impostures of Satan; but he calls the reading forced. He takes the clause as one sentence instead: the watchman, who ought to have been with God, is a snare of a fowler, the prophet showing what prophets ought to do rather than what they may do. The crime is thereby doubled and tripled, a man set on the watch-tower to be vigilant over the safety of the whole people being sharp-sighted only to snare them. Ellicott again offers another construction, that Ephraim is a lier-in-wait in conflict with my God; and since the objection lies in the Hebrew preposition, he suggests reading the word as people instead, so that Ephraim, the people of my God, is a lier-in-wait, a thought he finds full of pathos.
9:
How deep the corruption goes is stated first. Gill says the charge falls not on the false prophets only but on the ten tribes who through their means had degenerated, rooted in wickedness and incorrigible, so that there was no hope of reformation; they had reached the same pitch of uncleanness, barbarity and cruelty as the men of Gibeah in the matter of the Levite and his concubine. He reports a second reading from Jarchi, that Gibeah of Benjamin is meant as the place where the people asked a king and rebelled against the prophet. Clarke and Ellicott simply refer the reader to the history.

Calvin measures the depth with a figure. One who has fallen can raise himself when a hand is extended to him, and one who strives to emerge from the mire can plant his foot again on solid ground; but a man cast into a gulf has no hope of recovery, and the hand is extended in vain to one sinking in a shipwreck. So the people were unhealable, because their diseases had struck root too deeply to be cleansed. On the comparison itself Calvin says that Gibeah differed nothing from Sodom, that licentiousness prevailed there until there was no distinction between good and evil, and that the outrage brought on the slaughter which nearly demolished the tribe of Benjamin. What astonishes him is the place: a city taught in the law of God, near the destined site of the temple, abandoning itself to lusts filthier than the beasts. From the visiting that follows he draws two things, that the Lord will no longer spend labour in vain in teaching a people who count his teaching a mockery but will seize the sword, and that though he had hitherto spared them he had not forgotten the filth of their sins.

The grapes in the wilderness are taken by all as a figure of unearned favour. Wesley has God speak in the person of a traveller who unexpectedly finds a vine loaded with grapes; Clarke says that while they were faithful they were as acceptable to him as ripe grapes to a thirsty traveller; Ellicott explains the firstripe as the early fig which ripens in June while the rest come to maturity about August. Clarke names the fathers meant, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Joshua and Caleb, and reads the early fruit of a tree still in the vigour of youth as a metaphor of the rising prosperity of the state. Calvin guards the figure against a wrong inference. The prophet does not mean the people were worthy of being so much loved; the Hebrew word for finding is used as we say in French that a thing is to our taste, so that he relates not what God found in the people but reproves their ingratitude. Were any one to love me freely and I to slight him, Calvin says, it would be an evidence of pride and rudeness; and God does not merely love, but regards them as delectable fruit. Gill accommodates the same words to those called by grace, who in their natural state are as in a wilderness, and adds the caution that whatever good thing is in them at conversion is not found but put there.

The turn to Baal-peor is glossed from the older history. Ellicott identifies it as the place where Moabitic idolatry was practised and says the disgrace had burned itself into their national traditions and literature; he notes that the Hebrew word rendered shame was a euphemism for Baal, which is why names ending in that word are replaced by the older forms in Chronicles, and renders the last clause they have become abominations like their love. Clarke calls the idol the same as the Roman Priapus, worshipped with the most impure rites, and follows Newcome in rendering that they became as abominable as the object of their love.
11:
What the glory is that flies away is settled from the clauses that follow it. Gill canvasses three answers, that it means God himself departing from them, or their wealth and whatever was valuable among them flying away in a moment when they were carried captive, or rather their numerous posterity, in which they were fruitful according to their name and in which they gloried, children being the glory of their parents; he prefers the last because it agrees with what follows. Wesley says the same in a line, and Ellicott notes that progeny was the glory of ancient Israel. Henry frames the whole passage by the turn it makes: in the preceding verses the sin of Israel was derived from their fathers, and here the punishment of Israel is derived to their children, for as death entered by sin at first, so it is still entailed with it.

Which way the three terms run is disputed. Ellicott renders them so that there shall be no childbirth, nor pregnancy, nor conception, and calls this an ascending climax; Clarke follows Newcome in the same rendering and says that judgment blasts the very germs of population. Calvin reads them instead as gradations of a vengeance applied by degrees, so that if the first stroke leaves them still proud the Lord goes further back: the glory shall vanish from the birth, then they shall be slain in the womb, and at last, if they repent not, suffocated in the very conception. Keil and Delitzsch states the principle behind either reading, that the glory God gave his people through great multiplication shall vanish, and that the licentious worship of luxury will be punished by the diminution of their numbers, by childlessness, and by the destruction of such youth as may have grown up.

Calvin also warns against narrowing the sentence. He observes that the Hebrews often have abrupt sentences, and that the speech is striking here because the Lord names Ephraim and then breaks off rather than continuing the sense. He grants that according to the letter the prophet speaks of children, but holds that those who confine the sentence to offspring only are mistaken, since a part is taken for the whole, so that whatever was then deemed wealth or glory or power is included.

The next verse is read as closing the last opening left. Gill describes the case it allows for, of children carried in the womb to the full time, born, brought up to a more adult age, and appearing very promising to perpetuate the names of their fathers. Calvin says that even so it would be without advantage, since God would take away the youths in the flower of their age, and that entire destruction is thus threatened to the kingdom. Clarke and Wesley say briefly that the extirpation would be total.

The last clause is taken by several as the worst of the sentence. Wesley puts it plainly, that it is sad to lose our children but sadder to lose our God. Henry asks how a people who withdraw from their allegiance can expect anything but that he should depart from them and withdraw both his protection and his blessing. Calvin explains why the clause had to be added at all: wicked men dream that though God be displeased things will still go on prosperously with them, because they neither ascribe adversities to his wrath nor acknowledge the fountain of all blessings to be his free and paternal favour; so however much God proclaims that he is armed to destroy them, they care nothing and promise themselves a prosperous fortune until they feel his hand and the signs of destruction appear. Henry, ranging further down the chapter in the same note, passes on a conjecture he calls mystical, that the name of the place where the wickedness of the people was gathered answers in Syriac to Golgotha.
13:
What the comparison with Tyre asserts is not agreed. Gill offers two constructions: that as the prophet saw in vision that Tyre, for all its wealth, would be destroyed first by Nebuchadnezzar and then by Alexander, so he saw that the ten tribes, equal to Tyre in prosperity as the Targum has it, would be given up to ruin by the Assyrians; or else that the words mean Ephraim as I saw it reaching unto Tyre, bordering on that place as part of the ten tribes did. Clarke sets the two cities side by side, Tyre on a rock in the sea and Samaria on a mountain, and says the strength and beauty of neither shall save them. Ellicott calls the reference very obscure and reports that the old Greek suggests a doubt as to the validity of the text, rendering instead that Ephraim, even as I saw, gave their children for a prey; he notes that some render the Hebrew word for meadow by resting-place, giving I look on Ephraim even as I look on Tyre, planted in a sure resting-place, and observes that the fortress of Tyre was a conspicuous object in the days of Hosea, and Samaria too a stronghold able to resist prolonged sieges.

Calvin rejects the reading that makes the comparison a threat, that an event awaits this people like the one that befell Tyre; he calls it too refined. He supplies instead a word for tree or plant, so that Ephraim was as a tree planted in Tyre and kept in a dwelling. Tyre was built on an island and washed on every side by the sea, with gardens of the greatest pleasantness which were not formed without much expense and labour; raising trees there was a work in which men struggled with nature. The figure is of a tree preserved indoors, as trees that cannot bear the cold air are kept in a house through the winter. Behind it Calvin sets the reason the warning was needed, that prosperity is compared to wine because it inebriates men, or rather dementates them, and that the abuse of God's forbearance has destroyed almost all the reprobate, as Paul also says.

The prayer that follows is read by Clarke as interrupted in the middle. He finds an uncommon beauty in the words: the prophet begins to intercede, but having formed the first part of his petition the prophetic light discovered to him that it would not be answered and that God was about to give them something widely different; so he changes his petition and asks what it is that will be given, and the answer is put into his mouth to announce. Gill says the prophet's heart ached at the foreseen butchery but he was at a loss what to ask, their sins being so many and the decree already gone forth; he reports the rendering of Jarchi, Kimchi and Abarbinel, give them what thou wilt give them. Calvin rejects that rendering outright, saying those who translate give them what thou art about to give do not comprehend the design and are wholly mistaken, since the prophet is set before us as anxious and perplexed, reasoning with himself and with God about what is left to ask.

All agree that the request itself measures the calamity. Calvin observes that a numerous offspring is not the least of God's blessings, so that it is a token of dreadful judgement when barrenness, in itself a curse, is desired as an especial blessing; and he recalls that Christ said the barren would be blessed when the last destruction of Jerusalem came. Ellicott puts it as better universal childlessness than that the offspring should be exposed to so terrible a fate, and Wesley as less misery to have none than to have all our children murdered. Keil and Delitzsch reads what follows as the Lord's reply.
15:
Why Gilgal is named is answered from its past. Gill recalls that there the covenant of circumcision was renewed in Joshua's time, the first passover was kept in the land, and the tabernacle stood for a while; now all manner of iniquity was committed in it, and it was chosen by idolaters for the very reason that it had formerly been famous for religious worship. He adds that this was not to the exclusion of Dan and Bethel, and reports from Kimchi and Abarbinel that here began the first departure from the Lord in the asking of a king in the days of Samuel. Clarke grants that we are not directly informed of the fact, but says we have reason to believe scandalous practices of idolatry went on there. Wesley says that where they began to sin, there God began to show that he hated them.

Calvin explains why the whole wickedness of a nation can be located in one place. He takes the word all for what is chief or principal, and reads the sentence comparatively: sacrificing at Gilgal was more abominable in God's sight than adulteries, or plunder, or frauds, or unjust violence. The reason is that superstitious men, when reproved, bring forward their exercises of religion by way of compensation; and the Lord is far more grievously offended with such disguises than with a life void of every appearance of religion. What was a celebrated place they had turned into the seat of the basest impiety.

The house they are driven from is identified in two ways. Ellicott reports that Wünsche and Nowack interpret it, with considerable show of reason, as the holy land; he supports this from the Assyrian word answering to the Hebrew for house, which blended the conception of a people with the territory they occupied, and compares the naming of Egypt as the house of slaves. He also hears in the word an echo of the domestic story at the opening of the book, Ephraim being turned out of house and home like an adulterous wife. Clarke takes it of the household rather than the land, so that they should cease to be of the heavenly family, either as sons or servants.

The smitten tree is the last figure. Gill notes that they had flourished in the days of Jeroboam the second and were now like a tree beaten to pieces by lightning or hail, through civil wars and murders among themselves and the exactions of Pul and the depredations of Tiglathpileser. Keil and Delitzsch compares them to a plant so injured by the heat of the sun or by a worm that it dries up and bears no more fruit, and observes that the perfects are prophetic. Calvin says the tree has not only had its branches cut off but has been torn up from the roots, so that no residue should remain. Ellicott notes the irony that Ephraim, whose name means fruitfulness, shall bear none.

The closing words are read as the prophet taking sides. Calvin says that though worship was corrupted in that kingdom they still boasted themselves the holy seed of Abraham and had God's name ready in every mouth; so the prophet answers that he is no more your God, mine he is, setting himself alone against the whole people and bringing God forward as the defender of his doctrine. Gill makes the same point about the phrase my God. Clarke treats the verse as a vindication of the divine justice, the cause given being that they did not hearken; and on the wandering he admits that where they went no one can tell, reporting without endorsing a pious writer who thought their descendants were the American Indians. Ellicott says the word is strangely confirmed by the Assyrian monuments and by the whole later history of the people.
